dossier.public_summary: The dip is on the target star but its depth and shape change a lot between visits, and the star shows strong 2.16-day spot variations almost exactly at the 2.18-day dip period with a large phase swing. Together this matches a spotted or ellipsoidal variation on the star itself, not a stable planet transit.

reasons.why: Outside-eclipse swing is a large fraction of the dip depth with high chi2; points to a single, cool star varying at this period, not a planet transit.

Dip period is synchronous with the star's spot rotation (false_alarm 1.126959893144592e-291). A true transit would be unrelated to the rotation unless exactly synchronous as a tidally locked binary, strongly favouring stellar variability/EB.
reasons.value: rotation_d 2.169 signal_period_d 2.18479 signal_over_rotation 1.0072798524665745 amplitude_ppm 41659 in sector 9

reasons.why: Individual transit depths are highly inconsistent with a constant planet transit; signal is not repeatable noise.

Depth changes dramatically between sectors (sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source), as expected when a rotational modulation is sampled at different spot phases, not a stable planet.
reasons.value: p_constant 1.53e-11 depth_change_pct 162.7 sectors [1154 ppm, 525 ppm, 158 ppm]

reasons.why: Dip is on target and no neighbour within 1 pixel can plausibly cause it (closest 70 arcsec needing deep eclipse), so the variability is on the target itself, not a blended EB.
Independent scorer ranks this as much less planet-like than median planet; combined with the three diagnostics above, EB/rotational variability is best explanation.
